# "The Fundamentals" Do Not Require Decomposition or Prescription
**What it is** — The belief that basic skills must be isolated and explicitly taught before a player can use them in the game is not supported by head-to-head evidence. Three studies, cited by Myszka, Yearby and Gray:
- **Deuker et al. (2023), soccer.** Traditional decontextualised practice (dribbling around cones, passing through cones, shooting into an empty net, with prescriptive technical instruction and corrective feedback) versus a constraints-led approach using small-sided and conditioned games. Both groups were tested *on the out-of-context cone tests* — the traditional group's home ground. **No significant difference in improvement.** More striking: the traditional group took **777 ball touches** to produce those gains, the CLA group **354**. Roughly half the repetitions for the same result.
- **Esposito et al. (2024), soccer.** 30 players randomised to CLA or prescriptive training, assessed on the Loughborough Soccer Passing Test — again a decomposed, out-of-context technical test. **No significant group difference.**

# Contextual Sprint Work: Invite the Sprint, Don't Prescribe It
**What it is** — The authors' position on programmed speed work: **the majority of sprint work should take the form of contextually-driven movement problems** and the solutions that emerge from them. Since coaches are problem-setters who manipulate constraints to channel behaviour — including accelerating over a given distance — **they typically do not have players run sprints for the sake of it.** Instead they design so that sprinting appears as **an affordance** the player accepts within a contextual activity.
The specific recommendation: **place great emphasis on having opposing players chase from behind**, which changes the nature of the problem-solution dynamics.
**Why it works** — A sprint run for its own sake trains the action with the information removed ([[framework--three-types-of-task-decomposition]]). A sprint that occurs because a defender is closing is the same physical output coupled to the thing that regulates it in a game — which is the difference between near and far transfer ([[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]]) and the practical face of [[principle--gamespeed-vs-stopwatch-speed]].

# There Is No Muscle Memory, and the Brain Is Not a Computer
**What it is** — Davids and Araújo state it flatly: **"There is no such thing as 'muscle memory,' nor is this phrase a useful analogy for what goes on during skill learning. The brain is not a computer."** The body is a highly complex, interconnected biological system in which the brain plays a role in forming memories through synaptic and neuronal interconnections — one important part of a deeply integrated whole movement system, itself interconnected with an ever-changing environment.
The consequence they draw: **the athlete can never be understood, nor meaningfully considered, without reference to the environment, and vice versa.** Hence the need for an integrated athlete–environment scale of analysis.
**Why it works** — "Muscle memory" is not merely imprecise, it carries the cognitive-computational theory inside it: a stored program, written by repetition, that runs off on its own without attention. That picture is what justifies rote drilling, automaticity as the goal, and treating thought during performance as a burden to be lifted. Reject the metaphor and the training rationale attached to it loses its footing.

# Repetition Without Repetition
**What it is** — Bernstein's (1967) formulation, and the single most portable idea in the book. Ordinary repetition means rehearsing and reproducing a *technique*. **Repetition without repetition means repeatedly solving the same performance problem, challenged differently each time.** What repeats is the problem; what varies is the solution.
The authors are explicit that repetition itself is not the enemy — "while repetition is an important feature of practice, repetition without repetition is even better." And it can be **turbocharged by adding variability**: running the same task at different fatigue levels, or changing the performance context in a way that meaningfully challenges the player.
**Why it works** — Because no two problems on a field are ever the same, so no two solutions will be either. Practising one movement prepares one problem. Practising the *process* of solving prepares the class of problems. The player is, in the authors' phrase, **learning to learn to move** (Adolph & Hoch, 2019; Harlow, 1949) — the degrees of freedom of perception, cognition and action are repeatedly reorganised into different configurations that fit.

# Functional Variability
**What it is** — Variability in human movement is **inherently present** in neurobiological systems (Button et al., 2020; Chow et al., 2016), and it is **beneficial** for solving dynamic problems — which rejects the traditional project of teaching idealised patterns (Chow et al., 2006). Everyone is different and capable of solutions uniquely their own, so coaches should **inject variability into practice to encourage exploratory behaviour** — through purposeful constraint manipulation, or by encouraging athletes to search for different ways of solving the problem.
The word doing the work is **functional**. Variability is assessed by **how practical and useful the solution was in solving the problem** — not by how different it was.
**Why it works** — The chapter's worked example is unusually concrete. A group of defensive backs explore their coverage strategies — backpedal, shuffle (the 50/50 technique), angle breaks, zone and speed turns — against receivers running the routes and tactical situations they will actually see. Following Orth et al. (2017) on creative solutions emerging from exploration, the exploration happens at two levels:

# The Three Types of Task Decomposition
**What it is** — A diagnostic taxonomy for *how* a practice activity has been broken apart. Traditional practice decomposes skills for two reasons: to reduce cognitive load, and because you cannot always assemble a full team. It happens in three distinct ways:
1. **Perception-action decoupling** — severing the link between picking up information and acting on it. A back cutting around cones; a quarterback throwing through a tire; film-room progressions where the only "action" is saying what you would do; screen-based perceptual-cognitive tools where a complex field action is replaced by a tap.
2. **Part-task training** — dividing an action into movement *phases*. Two sub-types (Wickens et al., 2013): **segmentation** separates phases that occur in sequence (drilling the early and late cocking phases of a throw separately), **fractionation** separates phases that normally occur *simultaneously* (footwork drilled apart from throwing).

# Specificity of Adaptation

**What it is** — Adaptation is highly specific to the type of training undertaken. Training must therefore be built around the **energy systems**, **skills**, and **motor abilities** that dominate the target sport. The structural and physiological changes a body makes are dictated by the specific demands the athlete imposes — via the volume, intensity, and frequency of the activities pursued.

**Why it works** — Different stressors drive distinct adaptations: neuromuscular (motor-unit recruitment, firing rate, hypertrophy), metabolic (ATP/PCr/glycogen stores, lactate tolerance, glycolytic vs oxidative efficiency), and cardiorespiratory (stroke volume, capillary density, lactate threshold, V̇O₂max). You get back the specific quality you trained; the more complex the sport, the longer adaptation takes.

**When to apply** — Exercise and modality selection; justifying why general fitness must eventually yield to sport-specific work; matching the bioenergetic emphasis of a block to competition demands.

**When NOT to apply** — Specificity is not a mandate to train *only* the competition movement from day one — that conflicts with building a broad base first (see [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]). Early over-specialization narrows the foundation and raises injury risk. Specificity governs the *later*, sharper phases; the general-to-specific sequence still holds.

**Example** — A team-sport athlete needing repeated-sprint ability trains the glycolytic/PCr systems with short high-intensity intervals and change-of-direction work, rather than steady-state aerobic runs that would adapt the wrong energy system.

From 1998 to 2021 the literature accumulated **73 studies (1,824 participants) showing superior *performance* under external focus, and 40 studies (1,274 participants) showing better *learning*** (Chua et al., 2021). The benefits are durable — still present in retention tests 24 hours later — and they transfer to untrained tasks.
**Why it works** — Attending to your own body interferes with the self-organising control that produces the movement; attending to the outcome lets it organise itself around the goal. Porter et al. (2010) is the clean demonstration: participants ran an L-shaped cone course. Internal instructions ("focus on moving your legs as rapidly as possible", "plant your foot as firmly as possible") versus external ("focus on running toward the cone as rapidly as possible", "push off the ground as forcefully as possible"). Same task, near-identical wording — **350 ms faster under external focus.** Post-trial questioning confirmed the mechanism: body-referring instructions produced an internal focus on 76% of trials; environment-referring instructions, on 2%.
**When to apply** — Every cue, every session. It is the cheapest available upgrade to coaching practice: no equipment, no schedule change, only different words. It is also the easiest first change to sell to a sceptical coach, because it does not ask them to give up any drill.

# "The Fundamentals" Do Not Require Decomposition or Prescription
**What it is** — The belief that basic skills must be isolated and explicitly taught before a player can use them in the game is not supported by head-to-head evidence. Three studies, cited by Myszka, Yearby and Gray:
- **Deuker et al. (2023), soccer.** Traditional decontextualised practice (dribbling around cones, passing through cones, shooting into an empty net, with prescriptive technical instruction and corrective feedback) versus a constraints-led approach using small-sided and conditioned games. Both groups were tested *on the out-of-context cone tests* — the traditional group's home ground. **No significant difference in improvement.** More striking: the traditional group took **777 ball touches** to produce those gains, the CLA group **354**. Roughly half the repetitions for the same result.
- **Esposito et al. (2024), soccer.** 30 players randomised to CLA or prescriptive training, assessed on the Loughborough Soccer Passing Test — again a decomposed, out-of-context technical test. **No significant group difference.**

# Contextual Sprint Work: Invite the Sprint, Don't Prescribe It
**What it is** — The authors' position on programmed speed work: **the majority of sprint work should take the form of contextually-driven movement problems** and the solutions that emerge from them. Since coaches are problem-setters who manipulate constraints to channel behaviour — including accelerating over a given distance — **they typically do not have players run sprints for the sake of it.** Instead they design so that sprinting appears as **an affordance** the player accepts within a contextual activity.
The specific recommendation: **place great emphasis on having opposing players chase from behind**, which changes the nature of the problem-solution dynamics.
**Why it works** — A sprint run for its own sake trains the action with the information removed ([[framework--three-types-of-task-decomposition]]). A sprint that occurs because a defender is closing is the same physical output coupled to the thing that regulates it in a game — which is the difference between near and far transfer ([[principle--far-transfer-is-rare]]) and the practical face of [[principle--gamespeed-vs-stopwatch-speed]].

# There Is No Muscle Memory, and the Brain Is Not a Computer
**What it is** — Davids and Araújo state it flatly: **"There is no such thing as 'muscle memory,' nor is this phrase a useful analogy for what goes on during skill learning. The brain is not a computer."** The body is a highly complex, interconnected biological system in which the brain plays a role in forming memories through synaptic and neuronal interconnections — one important part of a deeply integrated whole movement system, itself interconnected with an ever-changing environment.
The consequence they draw: **the athlete can never be understood, nor meaningfully considered, without reference to the environment, and vice versa.** Hence the need for an integrated athlete–environment scale of analysis.
**Why it works** — "Muscle memory" is not merely imprecise, it carries the cognitive-computational theory inside it: a stored program, written by repetition, that runs off on its own without attention. That picture is what justifies rote drilling, automaticity as the goal, and treating thought during performance as a burden to be lifted. Reject the metaphor and the training rationale attached to it loses its footing.

# Repetition Without Repetition
**What it is** — Bernstein's (1967) formulation, and the single most portable idea in the book. Ordinary repetition means rehearsing and reproducing a *technique*. **Repetition without repetition means repeatedly solving the same performance problem, challenged differently each time.** What repeats is the problem; what varies is the solution.
The authors are explicit that repetition itself is not the enemy — "while repetition is an important feature of practice, repetition without repetition is even better." And it can be **turbocharged by adding variability**: running the same task at different fatigue levels, or changing the performance context in a way that meaningfully challenges the player.
**Why it works** — Because no two problems on a field are ever the same, so no two solutions will be either. Practising one movement prepares one problem. Practising the *process* of solving prepares the class of problems. The player is, in the authors' phrase, **learning to learn to move** (Adolph & Hoch, 2019; Harlow, 1949) — the degrees of freedom of perception, cognition and action are repeatedly reorganised into different configurations that fit.

# Functional Variability
**What it is** — Variability in human movement is **inherently present** in neurobiological systems (Button et al., 2020; Chow et al., 2016), and it is **beneficial** for solving dynamic problems — which rejects the traditional project of teaching idealised patterns (Chow et al., 2006). Everyone is different and capable of solutions uniquely their own, so coaches should **inject variability into practice to encourage exploratory behaviour** — through purposeful constraint manipulation, or by encouraging athletes to search for different ways of solving the problem.
The word doing the work is **functional**. Variability is assessed by **how practical and useful the solution was in solving the problem** — not by how different it was.
**Why it works** — The chapter's worked example is unusually concrete. A group of defensive backs explore their coverage strategies — backpedal, shuffle (the 50/50 technique), angle breaks, zone and speed turns — against receivers running the routes and tactical situations they will actually see. # The Three Types of Task Decomposition
**What it is** — A diagnostic taxonomy for *how* a practice activity has been broken apart. Traditional practice decomposes skills for two reasons: to reduce cognitive load, and because you cannot always assemble a full team. It happens in three distinct ways:
1. **Perception-action decoupling** — severing the link between picking up information and acting on it. A back cutting around cones; a quarterback throwing through a tire; film-room progressions where the only "action" is saying what you would do; screen-based perceptual-cognitive tools where a complex field action is replaced by a tap.
2. **Part-task training** — dividing an action into movement *phases*. Two sub-types (Wickens et al., 2013): **segmentation** separates phases that occur in sequence (drilling the early and late cocking phases of a throw separately), **fractionation** separates phases that normally occur *simultaneously* (footwork drilled apart from throwing).

# Specificity of Adaptation

**What it is** — Adaptation is highly specific to the type of training undertaken. Training must therefore be built around the **energy systems**, **skills**, and **motor abilities** that dominate the target sport. The structural and physiological changes a body makes are dictated by the specific demands the athlete imposes — via the volume, intensity, and frequency of the activities pursued.

**Why it works** — Different stressors drive distinct adaptations: neuromuscular (motor-unit recruitment, firing rate, hypertrophy), metabolic (ATP/PCr/glycogen stores, lactate tolerance, glycolytic vs oxidative efficiency), and cardiorespiratory (stroke volume, capillary density, lactate threshold, V̇O₂max). You get back the specific quality you trained; the more complex the sport, the longer adaptation takes.

**When to apply** — Exercise and modality selection; justifying why general fitness must eventually yield to sport-specific work; matching the bioenergetic emphasis of a block to competition demands.

**When NOT to apply** — Specificity is not a mandate to train *only* the competition movement from day one — that conflicts with building a broad base first (see [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]). Early over-specialization narrows the foundation and raises injury risk. Specificity governs the *later*, sharper phases; the general-to-specific sequence still holds.

**Example** — A team-sport athlete needing repeated-sprint ability trains the glycolytic/PCr systems with short high-intensity intervals and change-of-direction work, rather than steady-state aerobic runs that would adapt the wrong energy system.

# Two Kinds of Transfer: Physical Ability vs. Motor Skill

**What it is** — Moyer frames every exercise-selection argument as a transfer-of-training question and splits transfer into two kinds that get argued as if they were one. **Physical-ability transfer** asks whether getting stronger or more powerful carries over to sprinting ("does squatting make you faster?"). **Motor-skill transfer** asks whether an exercise changes *how* the athlete sprints: thigh height, pawback, foot contact. Both are graded the usual way: **positive** (training helps the target), **negative** (training hinders it), **zero** (no effect), and **near vs. far** (how similar the training context is to the target). Three things drive transfer: movement similarity, sensory similarity and cognitive factors. His central claim, taken from Bondarchuk, is that **motor-skill transfer is more specific than physical-ability transfer.** An exercise can build useful capacity and still leave technique untouched. Exercises are judged by the outcome they produce in the sprint, not by how hard or impressive they look.

**Why it works** — The mechanism he offers is the theory of identical elements (Thorndike & Woodworth, 1901): transfer scales with the number of elements two tasks share. Force capacity is a shared element for many tasks. A coordination pattern is shared only with tasks that have the same joint actions, timing and sensory feedback, so skill transfer drops off faster with distance. This is asserted from the Soviet transfer literature and educational psychology. The course does not show the data.

**When to apply** — Settling "does X transfer to speed?" arguments on a staff: first ask *which* transfer is meant. # Bondarchuk's Four Exercise Categories, Applied to Sprinting

**What it is** — The classic three-way split (general preparatory / special preparatory / competitive, in use for "more than 100 years" per Moyer) was refined by Bondarchuk into four classes, each defined by how much of the competition movement it reproduces:

| Class | Definition (as Moyer gives it) | Sprint examples from the course |
|---|---|---|
| **General preparatory (GPE)** | Resembles no part of the competition movement; for all-round conditioning and recovery | General conditioning, recovery work |
| **Special preparatory (SPE)** | Does not copy the event's movement but trains the same muscle groups and physiological systems | Max strength, Olympic lifts, jumps, med-ball throws. **The clean goes here.** Moyer says sprinting has no "triple extension", so a clean's recruitment resembles sprinting but its movement does not |
| **Special developmental (SDE)** | Repeats part or all of the competition event, usually against resistance | Band-resisted knee drive, band-resisted pawback, bounding, "ball under" knee-drive work |
| **Competition (CE)** | The whole event, with lighter or heavier loads | Sprinting itself; sprinting with light wearable resistance; (by analogy) throwing lighter balls |

**Why it works** — It puts the theory of identical elements into practice (see [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]). The further down the table, the more elements the exercise shares with the sprint and the higher the chance of *skill* transfer. The higher up the table, the more the exercise builds general capacity with skill transfer unlikely. Bondarchuk's refinement matters because he found parts of "general" and "special" work can still transfer depending on the block and the athlete. Moyer asserts the mechanism. The data behind it are Bondarchuk's, and the course only summarises them.

**When to apply** — Auditing a college football speed/strength program: label every exercise GPE/SPE/SDE/CE and check the mix fits the phase. In summer you might expect SPE-heavy work with some SDE. In fall camp, CE (sprinting) and SDE should lead. In RTP after a hamstring strain, the classes give a ready progression: GPE/SPE for tissue capacity → SDE (banded pawback, isometric hamstring work in sprint positions) → CE (sprinting, then sprinting with light external load).

**When NOT to apply** — The classes describe *movement* similarity only. They say nothing about perceptual similarity. A CE-class 40-yard sprint is still decontextualised from game running, where a receiver sprints relative to a DB and a ball (see the Myszka entries). Class boundaries are fuzzy. Moyer's "no triple extension in sprinting" is a contested biomechanics claim being used to place the clean in a class. And the table does not tell you the *dose* of each class. That is the separate unification principle.

**Example** — A wideout's June week: trap-bar and hang clean (SPE), banded knee-drive and pawback (SDE), and wicket runs plus flying sprints (CE). In August the SPE volume drops and the CE share rises, but no class disappears.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] — agree that later phases sharpen toward the competition movement; Moyer's four classes give a finer grain than Bompa's general→specific sequence.

# Unify General and Special Means in the Same Period

**What it is** — Moyer's reading of the Soviet "principle of unifying general and special preparation" (1940s–50s onward; quoted from Matveyev, 1978): general and special means are **both essential and must coexist**, and excluding either would be "devastating to the multi-year system." The point he stresses is that this is not only a multi-year sequence (general first, then specific). **Both are present in the same training period.** Only their proportion changes. He uses the image of dimmer switches: in a general-emphasis block the special work is still there at a lower level, and as competition approaches the two dials swap. Matveyev notes the right ratio is individual and changes over time: some athletes need steadily less general work, others more. Most coaches agree that as qualification rises, general volume falls "somewhat" and special volume rises.

**Why it works** — General means build the capacity that special means convert. Special means keep the skill and its specific coordination from decaying while capacity is built. If you split them into consecutive blocks, whichever quality is not trained detrains, and the athlete has to re-couple capacity and skill late. This mechanism is the Soviet authors' rationale as Moyer relays it. He cites no outcome data.

**When to apply** — College football's year makes this concrete. Winter/summer are general-emphasis but should still carry sprint technique work (SDE/CE) at low volume. Camp and in-season are special-emphasis but still need a general strength dose to hold capacity. In RTP it argues against "gym phase, then running phase." Start low-intensity sprint-technique exposure (marching, wickets at submaximal speed) while tissue capacity is still being rebuilt, as far as tissue tolerance allows.

**When NOT to apply** — Early rehab can legitimately be almost all general because the tissue cannot tolerate special loading yet. Unification is a goal once tolerance allows, not a rule that overrides medical staging. It is also not a prescription for ratios. Moyer gives none, and the right mix for an 18-year-old freshman versus a fifth-year senior differs, which is exactly Matveyev's point. Moyer's aside that high-school programs "still" run pure general-then-specific is his characterisation, not a survey.

**Example** — A redshirt freshman corner in January: most sessions are strength and hypertrophy, but every session opens with 10 minutes of wickets and banded pawbacks. By August the proportions have flipped. Sprinting and special strength lead, and two short heavy lifts a week hold capacity.

**Related** — [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]] — tension: Bompa sequences general before specific over the career; Moyer insists both run concurrently within a period (compatible at the multi-year scale, in conflict if "sequence" is read as block-by-block). Also [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]].

# "Exercise Selection Matters More Than Intensity and Volume"

**What it is** — Moyer's loudest claim in Lesson 8 ("let me say that a little bit louder for the people in the back"), attributed to Bondarchuk's transfer-of-training work. **Exercise selection matters more for transfer than intensity or volume.** From it he draws a practical rule, which he credits to Bondarchuk, Issurin and Natalia Verkhoshansky: **find the exercises that transfer, then build as many variations of those exercises as possible.** Pushing harder or doing more of a non-transferring exercise is not the answer. The supporting story: Bondarchuk collected **over 7,000 questionnaires** from Soviet athletes and coaches and found that as athletes improved in general exercises their competition results began to decline. The best competition performers were not always the best at individual general exercises, so "specialized exercises were the key to success."

**Why it works** — The mechanism offered is transfer specificity. If an exercise shares few elements with the sprint, adding load or volume only adds adaptation that does not carry over. Bondarchuk goes further (quoted): developing "unnecessary muscle groups" has unavoidable negative effects in speed-strength events. Variations of a transferring exercise are said to keep the stimulus new (Zatsiorsky's third load lever, "novelty", alongside intensity and volume) without leaving the transferring movement.

**When to apply** — As a design prompt, not a law. When a football player's speed has stalled despite rising strength numbers, look at *what* he does before *how much*. Build variation families around exercises that visibly change sprint mechanics: banded knee drive → cycled → with wearable load → explosive front lunge with knee drive.

**When NOT to apply** — This is `untested` for three reasons. (1) The evidence is a retrospective questionnaire study reported second-hand. Moyer does not give its design, and correlation between general-lift gains and competition decline has obvious confounders (training age, specialisation timing, the decline in general work that normally comes with qualification). (2) Bondarchuk's population was elite Soviet throwers and speed-strength athletes, not collision-sport players who also need mass and contact tolerance. (3) "More important than intensity and volume" is a comparison no controlled study in the course tests. For football, strength and body mass are performance and injury-tolerance ends in themselves, so demoting intensity/volume can under-build a lineman or a player returning from a long layoff.

**Example** — A slot receiver's back squat rose 40 lb over winter while his fly-10 stayed flat. Under this claim, the next block keeps the squat at maintenance and puts the new time into a variation family of pawback and knee-drive special exercises. Whether the fly-10 then moves is the test. The claim itself does not guarantee it.

**Related** — [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]; [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] — tension: Bompa treats load progression as the primary driver of adaptation; Moyer/Bondarchuk rank selection above load for transfer.

# Unify General and Special Means in the Same Period

**What it is** — Moyer's reading of the Soviet "principle of unifying general and special preparation" (1940s–50s onward; quoted from Matveyev, 1978): general and special means are **both essential and must coexist**, and excluding either would be "devastating to the multi-year system." The point he stresses is that this is not only a multi-year sequence (general first, then specific). **Both are present in the same training period.** Only their proportion changes. He uses the image of dimmer switches: in a general-emphasis block the special work is still there at a lower level, and as competition approaches the two dials swap. Matveyev notes the right ratio is individual and changes over time: some athletes need steadily less general work, others more. Most coaches agree that as qualification rises, general volume falls "somewhat" and special volume rises.

**Why it works** — General means build the capacity that special means convert. Special means keep the skill and its specific coordination from decaying while capacity is built. If you split them into consecutive blocks, whichever quality is not trained detrains, and the athlete has to re-couple capacity and skill late. This mechanism is the Soviet authors' rationale as Moyer relays it. He cites no outcome data.

**When to apply** — College football's year makes this concrete. Winter/summer are general-emphasis but should still carry sprint technique work (SDE/CE) at low volume. Camp and in-season are special-emphasis but still need a general strength dose to hold capacity. In RTP it argues against "gym phase, then running phase." Start low-intensity sprint-technique exposure (marching, wickets at submaximal speed) while tissue capacity is still being rebuilt, as far as tissue tolerance allows.

**When NOT to apply** — Early rehab can legitimately be almost all general because the tissue cannot tolerate special loading yet. Unification is a goal once tolerance allows, not a rule that overrides medical staging. It is also not a prescription for ratios. Moyer gives none, and the right mix for an 18-year-old freshman versus a fifth-year senior differs, which is exactly Matveyev's point. Moyer's aside that high-school programs "still" run pure general-then-specific is his characterisation, not a survey.

**Example** — A redshirt freshman corner in January: most sessions are strength and hypertrophy, but every session opens with 10 minutes of wickets and banded pawbacks. By August the proportions have flipped. Sprinting and special strength lead, and two short heavy lifts a week hold capacity.

**Related** — [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]] — tension: Bompa sequences general before specific over the career; Moyer insists both run concurrently within a period (compatible at the multi-year scale, in conflict if "sequence" is read as block-by-block). Also [[principle--specificity-of-adaptation]].

# "Exercise Selection Matters More Than Intensity and Volume"

**What it is** — Moyer's loudest claim in Lesson 8 ("let me say that a little bit louder for the people in the back"), attributed to Bondarchuk's transfer-of-training work. **Exercise selection matters more for transfer than intensity or volume.** From it he draws a practical rule, which he credits to Bondarchuk, Issurin and Natalia Verkhoshansky: **find the exercises that transfer, then build as many variations of those exercises as possible.** Pushing harder or doing more of a non-transferring exercise is not the answer. The supporting story: Bondarchuk collected **over 7,000 questionnaires** from Soviet athletes and coaches and found that as athletes improved in general exercises their competition results began to decline. The best competition performers were not always the best at individual general exercises, so "specialized exercises were the key to success."

**Why it works** — The mechanism offered is transfer specificity. If an exercise shares few elements with the sprint, adding load or volume only adds adaptation that does not carry over. Bondarchuk goes further (quoted): developing "unnecessary muscle groups" has unavoidable negative effects in speed-strength events. Variations of a transferring exercise are said to keep the stimulus new (Zatsiorsky's third load lever, "novelty", alongside intensity and volume) without leaving the transferring movement.

**When to apply** — As a design prompt, not a law. When a football player's speed has stalled despite rising strength numbers, look at *what* he does before *how much*. Build variation families around exercises that visibly change sprint mechanics: banded knee drive → cycled → with wearable load → explosive front lunge with knee drive.

**When NOT to apply** — This is `untested` for three reasons. (1) The evidence is a retrospective questionnaire study reported second-hand. Moyer does not give its design, and correlation between general-lift gains and competition decline has obvious confounders (training age, specialisation timing, the decline in general work that normally comes with qualification). (2) Bondarchuk's population was elite Soviet throwers and speed-strength athletes, not collision-sport players who also need mass and contact tolerance. (3) "More important than intensity and volume" is a comparison no controlled study in the course tests. For football, strength and body mass are performance and injury-tolerance ends in themselves, so demoting intensity/volume can under-build a lineman or a player returning from a long layoff.

**Example** — A slot receiver's back squat rose 40 lb over winter while his fly-10 stayed flat. Under this claim, the next block keeps the squat at maintenance and puts the new time into a variation family of pawback and knee-drive special exercises. Whether the fly-10 then moves is the test. The claim itself does not guarantee it.

# Accentuation: Load the Knee Drive and Pawback Where the Sprint Needs Force

**What it is** — The principle of accentuation (Zatsiorsky, *Science and Practice of Strength Training*), which Moyer uses as the design rule for special strength exercises: **train strength through the part of the range where the sport movement needs maximal force**, not through the full anatomical range. In running, muscles are active over a narrow range, and peak activity is near the end-points of angular motion. Zatsiorsky's own example is the swing leg: hip flexion is accentuated *before* the thigh reaches vertical and decelerated after it. So there is no reason to build hip-flexor strength beyond that range, or at the weakest position (as the "peak contraction principle" would suggest), because in that range the *extensors*, not the flexors, are working. The two band exercises that follow from it, and their setup rules:
- **Knee drive** — band anchored at **knee height**. The athlete starts with the thigh *behind* the body, folds the leg, and drives the thigh forward.
- **Pawback** — band anchored **high enough that the foot travels back *and down***, not just back, because that is the path of the foot into the ground when sprinting. Cue: "whip from the hip." For acceleration the variation starts thigh-up and attacks down. For upright running it is cycled quickly from a leg-out-front start.
- Verkhoshansky's 1986 demonstration (shown in Lesson 8) combines both actions in one exercise. In Live 3, Moyer shows a weighted-foot-strap ("Monkey Feet") version of it.

**Why it works** — Strength is joint-angle specific. Loading a movement where the sprint loads it gives more shared elements (see [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]) and less wasted work. The band's line of pull decides which part of the range is loaded, so the anchor height is not a detail. It *is* the exercise. The angle-specificity mechanism is textbook. That these particular band setups transfer to sprint mechanics is Moyer's practice claim.

**When to apply** — Programming hip-flexor and hamstring special strength for skill players. Late-stage hamstring RTP, where the goal moves from isolated capacity to force in sprint-relevant positions. Checking an existing banded drill: if the band pulls straight back at ankle height, the pawback is training "back" but not "down."

**When NOT to apply** — Accentuation is a transfer principle, not a rehab-capacity principle. Early after a hamstring strain, long-length and full-range work may be exactly what is needed even though the sprint never "uses" that range. Full-range work also restores the passive/active range the correctives menu depends on. Band tension also rises through the pull, so the load profile is not a true replica of the sprint. And "no reason to train the weakest position" should not be read as "never train it."

**Example** — A tailback who drops his foot straight down: banded pawback with the anchor raised from ankle to mid-shin height, 3×8 per side cycled fast, straight into 3 wicket runs so he can feel the back-and-down path at speed.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]] — these are the switching-quality strength exercises in that menu.

# Light Wearable Resistance "Out-Energises" a Heavy Squat — Claim, and Why the Numbers Fail

**What it is** — Moyer argues that very light, limb-mounted wearable resistance (LILA Exogen, loads "only in grams") is unusually powerful for sprint technique and speed. His mechanism is kinetic energy. As spoken in Lesson 8: a **100 kg back squat** gives kinetic energy of **"17.4 kg meters per second"**, while **one gram of LILA on the calves** gives **"18.6 kg per meter per second."** A barbell moves at about 1 m/s even in "speed squats", whereas the load on a sprinting limb moves at sprint speed ("eight, nine, ten meters per second"). So wearable load "keeps acceleration high" and "flips the force equation on its head." He cites John Cronin's work on upper- and lower-body wearable loading and acceleration kinematics as support. In Live 3 [00:00:01] he **retracts the arithmetic**: "Sorry, I fucked up the physics equation for the Lila's... that was Dr. John Cronin that did that so you can ask him." He keeps the conclusion.

**Why it works (as asserted)** — Kinetic energy is ½mv². Velocity is squared, so a small mass moving fast can carry energy comparable to a large mass moving slowly. Loading the distal limb also raises the limb's moment of inertia about the hip, which increases the demand on the hip flexors, the hamstrings and the knee drive and pawback ("load the problem"). That second mechanism is plausible and matches the placement rules in [[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]]. It is not the energy argument, though.

**When to apply** — As a hypothesis to test, with realistic loads: a small, placement-specific overload of the swing limb at sprint speed. Useful as a CE-class tool ([[framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories]]) when you want sprint-speed overload without a sled changing posture.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not repeat the squat-vs-wearable comparison. It is wrong in three separate ways. (1) **Units:** "kg·m/s" is momentum, not energy (energy is joules, kg·m²/s²). (2) **Magnitude:** 17.4 J for 100 kg implies a bar speed of ~0.59 m/s, which is plausible. But 18.6 J from **1 g** needs a limb speed of about **190 m/s**. Even at a realistic peak foot speed (~20 m/s), 1 g carries ~0.2 J, and a heavier real load (~200 g) carries tens of joules. The comparison is dimensionally and numerically inconsistent as spoken. (3) **Concept:** "acceleration of 8–9 m/s" confuses velocity with acceleration. Beyond the physics, "faster sprinting from wearable resistance" is a transfer claim: Cronin's studies (not checked here) describe acute kinematic and kinetic changes, and acute change is not proof of chronic speed gains. **Conflict of interest:** Moyer uses and promotes LILA heavily ("yes, those are my Lila's"), and the course's `_book.md` notes that he sells wearable-resistance coaching. Supporting cases are single athletes with other interventions running at the same time ([[case-study--nfl-running-back-long-lever-wearable-resistance-sprint]]).

**Example** — A staff member proposes buying wearable-resistance kits for the WR room because "a few grams beats a 100 kg squat." The correct response: the physics claim is broken. The limb-inertia mechanism is plausible. The purchase should hinge on a within-athlete trial with a measured outcome (fly-10, contact position on film), not the energy slide.

So there is no reason to build hip-flexor strength beyond that range, or at the weakest position (as the "peak contraction principle" would suggest), because in that range the *extensors*, not the flexors, are working. The two band exercises that follow from it, and their setup rules:
- **Knee drive** — band anchored at **knee height**. The athlete starts with the thigh *behind* the body, folds the leg, and drives the thigh forward.
- **Pawback** — band anchored **high enough that the foot travels back *and down***, not just back, because that is the path of the foot into the ground when sprinting. Cue: "whip from the hip." For acceleration the variation starts thigh-up and attacks down. For upright running it is cycled quickly from a leg-out-front start.
- Verkhoshansky's 1986 demonstration (shown in Lesson 8) combines both actions in one exercise. In Live 3, Moyer shows a weighted-foot-strap ("Monkey Feet") version of it.

**Why it works** — Strength is joint-angle specific. Loading a movement where the sprint loads it gives more shared elements (see [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]) and less wasted work. The band's line of pull decides which part of the range is loaded, so the anchor height is not a detail. It *is* the exercise. The angle-specificity mechanism is textbook. That these particular band setups transfer to sprint mechanics is Moyer's practice claim.

**When to apply** — Programming hip-flexor and hamstring special strength for skill players. Late-stage hamstring RTP, where the goal moves from isolated capacity to force in sprint-relevant positions. Checking an existing banded drill: if the band pulls straight back at ankle height, the pawback is training "back" but not "down."

**When NOT to apply** — Accentuation is a transfer principle, not a rehab-capacity principle. Early after a hamstring strain, long-length and full-range work may be exactly what is needed even though the sprint never "uses" that range. Full-range work also restores the passive/active range the correctives menu depends on. Band tension also rises through the pull, so the load profile is not a true replica of the sprint. And "no reason to train the weakest position" should not be read as "never train it."

**Example** — A tailback who drops his foot straight down: banded pawback with the anchor raised from ankle to mid-shin height, 3×8 per side cycled fast, straight into 3 wicket runs so he can feel the back-and-down path at speed.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]] — these are the switching-quality strength exercises in that menu.

# Light Wearable Resistance "Out-Energises" a Heavy Squat — Claim, and Why the Numbers Fail

**What it is** — Moyer argues that very light, limb-mounted wearable resistance (LILA Exogen, loads "only in grams") is unusually powerful for sprint technique and speed. His mechanism is kinetic energy. As spoken in Lesson 8: a **100 kg back squat** gives kinetic energy of **"17.4 kg meters per second"**, while **one gram of LILA on the calves** gives **"18.6 kg per meter per second."** A barbell moves at about 1 m/s even in "speed squats", whereas the load on a sprinting limb moves at sprint speed ("eight, nine, ten meters per second"). So wearable load "keeps acceleration high" and "flips the force equation on its head." He cites John Cronin's work on upper- and lower-body wearable loading and acceleration kinematics as support. In Live 3 [00:00:01] he **retracts the arithmetic**: "Sorry, I fucked up the physics equation for the Lila's... that was Dr. John Cronin that did that so you can ask him." He keeps the conclusion.

**Why it works (as asserted)** — Kinetic energy is ½mv². Velocity is squared, so a small mass moving fast can carry energy comparable to a large mass moving slowly. Loading the distal limb also raises the limb's moment of inertia about the hip, which increases the demand on the hip flexors, the hamstrings and the knee drive and pawback ("load the problem"). That second mechanism is plausible and matches the placement rules in [[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]]. It is not the energy argument, though.

**When to apply** — As a hypothesis to test, with realistic loads: a small, placement-specific overload of the swing limb at sprint speed. Useful as a CE-class tool ([[framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories]]) when you want sprint-speed overload without a sled changing posture.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not repeat the squat-vs-wearable comparison. It is wrong in three separate ways. (1) **Units:** "kg·m/s" is momentum, not energy (energy is joules, kg·m²/s²). (2) **Magnitude:** 17.4 J for 100 kg implies a bar speed of ~0.59 m/s, which is plausible. But 18.6 J from **1 g** needs a limb speed of about **190 m/s**. Even at a realistic peak foot speed (~20 m/s), 1 g carries ~0.2 J, and a heavier real load (~200 g) carries tens of joules. The comparison is dimensionally and numerically inconsistent as spoken. (3) **Concept:** "acceleration of 8–9 m/s" confuses velocity with acceleration. Beyond the physics, "faster sprinting from wearable resistance" is a transfer claim: Cronin's studies (not checked here) describe acute kinematic and kinetic changes, and acute change is not proof of chronic speed gains. **Conflict of interest:** Moyer uses and promotes LILA heavily ("yes, those are my Lila's"), and the course's `_book.md` notes that he sells wearable-resistance coaching. Supporting cases are single athletes with other interventions running at the same time ([[case-study--nfl-running-back-long-lever-wearable-resistance-sprint]]).

**Example** — A staff member proposes buying wearable-resistance kits for the WR room because "a few grams beats a 100 kg squat." The correct response: the physics claim is broken. The limb-inertia mechanism is plausible. The purchase should hinge on a within-athlete trial with a measured outcome (fly-10, contact position on film), not the energy slide.

# Match the Sprint Fault to a Range-of-Motion Check Before Choosing the Fix

**What it is** — Moyer does not go straight from a film fault to a drill. He first asks whether the athlete *can* reach the position, by checking passive and then active range at the joints that feed that fault. His mapping (lesson 6, with the tests shown in live session 3):
- **Poor projection / stands up early** → hip extension (he likes the Thomas test), ankle dorsiflexion, ankle plantar flexion, big-toe extension. Example: a soccer player who could barely lift his toes onto a yoga block ran exactly like that.
- **Long lever / poor fold-up** → active knee flexion in prone: can the athlete lift the heel toward the buttock with the hamstrings? He accepts a gap of about a pinky-to-thumb span; more than that needs work. He says this check is missing from the hamstring literature.
- **Straight knee at toe-off / poor ankle extension** → calf strength and ankle range (his reading; disputed).
- **Rotation at toe-off, not reaching the big toe** → hip, ankle or foot — check all three.
- **Dorsiflexion** → knee-to-wall, heel staying heavy and knee tracking over the **third** toe (not collapsing inward); he uses about 4 in from the wall as "adequate" and cites 20° as the usual target.

**Why it works** — A fault can come from a capacity limit (range, strength) or from coordination. A cue or drill cannot fix a range limit, and range work will not fix a timing problem. Checking first keeps the intervention matched to the cause.

**When to apply** — After the film review and before writing the individual block; in RTP, where the medical staff already record range, share the numbers rather than re-testing.

**When NOT to apply** — The mapping is Moyer's reasoning, **not a validated diagnostic chain**: normal range does not rule out a range contribution at sprint speed, and a range deficit does not prove it causes the fault. His thresholds are rough (a hand-span, "about 4 inches") and he admits they are not scientific. Treat a limited joint as a hypothesis to test by re-filming after the range improves.

**Example** — A defensive end shows little thigh spread and rises by 5 yd. His Thomas test shows a hip flexor limit and his knee-to-wall is 2 in. Staff add loaded hip-extension and ankle range work for three weeks before adding any projection drills, then re-film.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-fault-observation-checklist]] — the faults this check follows.

# NFL Running Back With a Long Swing Lever: ROM Work, Posterior-Calf Loading, Wickets

**What it is** — Moyer's flagship single-athlete case, told in Lesson 8 and filled in during Live 3, where the athlete is named as Najee Harris ("Naji" in the transcript). The athlete was an NFL running back, **245 lb** (the transcript also says "fixed two", probably a height such as 6'2"; unclear). **Problem:** he swung a long lever with one leg (Live 3 says the left). He struggled to fold the leg and struggled with knee-drive exercises. **Assessment (Live 3):** his active hamstring range was very poor: he could not lift his heel toward his butt with the hamstrings in prone, and the gap was well beyond Moyer's pinky-to-thumb threshold ([[framework--sprint-rom-screen-thomas-hamstring-dorsiflexion]]). **Interventions** reported across the two lessons: hamstring PAILs/RAILs to close the active–passive gap; LILA calf sleeves loaded on the **posterior calf** ("load the problem"; his thighs were too big for the shorts); knee-drive special strength; and wicket runs, which the athlete asked for as a former high-school track athlete, later faded by removing hurdles and combined with wearable load. **Reported outcome (Lesson 8):** in **one month**, his **flying-10** time improved by what the transcript renders as "500th" (most likely five hundredths of a second; unconfirmed), "doing nothing but sprinting and using Lila's." On film the lever shortened. He liked the sleeves enough to wear them in NFL practices.

**Why it works (as claimed)** — Moyer's account: the posterior-calf load increases the demand on the hamstrings to fold the leg and on the ankle, and the extra sensory input makes the fold something the athlete can feel. PAILs/RAILs gave him the active range to fold at all. Wickets use the fear of clipping a hurdle to force front-side mechanics without a cue.

**When to apply** — As a template of *reasoning* for a football player with a long lever: film → check active vs. passive hamstring and hip-flexion range → close the range gap → strength in range → a constraint that forces the fold → fade the constraint → re-time. The order transfers well to RTP after a hamstring strain, where a long lever is also one of Moyer's hamstring-risk hypotheses.

**When NOT to apply** — Not evidence that wearable resistance works. It is one athlete. The Lesson 8 phrase "doing nothing but sprinting and using Lila's" conflicts with the Live 3 account of PAILs/RAILs, knee drives and wickets. There was no control, no stated timing method, and a flying-10 change of ~0.05 s is within the day-to-day variation of many timing setups. A month of focused sprinting alone would be expected to help an NFL back coming off a season. The equipment is Moyer's own, and he promotes the product. The athlete is identifiable. Cite the reasoning, not the result.

**Example** — Baylor application: a transfer RB with a visible long lever on the left and a hamstring history gets the same sequence. He gets prone active knee-flexion testing, a PAILs/RAILs block, posterior-calf loading on selected sprints, and wickets with a planned fade. Fly-10 is timed on the same system before and after, with the other changes logged so the result is interpretable.

**Related** — [[claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]]; [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]] — the risk hypothesis this case is used to illustrate.

# The Passive-vs-Active Range Rule: What the Gap Tells You to Train

**What it is** — Moyer's triage rule for any sprint fault that could have a range-of-motion cause. Test the relevant joint **passively** (you move it) and **actively** (the athlete moves it under their own muscle), then branch:
1. **Passive range is lacking** → address the range first (loaded stretches, "time and/or tension"). "First and foremost, they have to have passive. That's number one."
2. **Passive range is adequate but active falls short** (you can lift the thigh high; they cannot) → the gap "should be filled with specific strength exercises": **strength in that range** (PAILs/RAILs, isometrics at end range, special strength exercises).
3. **Both are adequate** → range is not the limiter. It is a strength, coordination or learning issue: technical drills, strength exercises, cues and wearable-load placement ([[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]]).
The goal is to make passive and active "as close to each other as possible — it's never going to be a perfect one to one."

**Why it works** — Passive range tells you whether the tissue and joint *allow* the position. Active range tells you whether the athlete can *produce and control* it. A sprint needs the active version at speed. A drill cannot give range the tissue does not have, and stretching cannot give control the nervous system and muscle cannot produce. The rule matches each deficit to the fix that can plausibly change it. The logic is standard in rehab. Moyer's range-gap training methods come from the FRC/FRS system (see [[heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint]]).

**When to apply** — Before prescribing any sprint corrective for projection (hip extension, ankle, big toe), switching (hamstring at the knee and hip flexion for a long lever), or toe-off (dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, tibial rotation). In RTP, it gives a clean hand-off: the athletic trainer or PT owns branch 1, and Athletic Performance owns branches 2–3 once passive range is restored. It also prevents wasted weeks of drills on an athlete who physically cannot reach the position.

**When NOT to apply** — Reactivity/stiffness faults are usually not range problems. Moyer himself says range "isn't usually going to be a problem" there; it is a strength-quality issue. Range measured on a table is slow and unloaded, so adequate numbers do not guarantee the range is available at sprint speed and fatigue. Moyer gives no validated cut-offs for "adequate" or for an acceptable gap. In the acute phase after injury, a passive–active gap may be protective, and loading end range is a medical decision.

**Example** — A safety cannot fold his swing leg. Prone passive knee flexion: heel to butt, fine. Active: heel stops a hand-span short. That is branch 2, so he gets hamstring PAILs/RAILs and GHR variations, not more butt-kick drills and not more stretching.

**Related** — [[heuristic--match-sprint-fault-to-rom-check-before-intervening]] — that entry maps which joint to check for each fault; this one says what to do with the result.

# The Passive-vs-Active Range Rule: What the Gap Tells You to Train

**What it is** — Moyer's triage rule for any sprint fault that could have a range-of-motion cause. Test the relevant joint **passively** (you move it) and **actively** (the athlete moves it under their own muscle), then branch:

# Moyer's Sprint ROM Screen: How He Runs Each Test and What He Watches For

**What it is** — The test procedures Moyer demonstrates in Live Teaching 3 (~19–28 min). Each is done **passive first, then active**. The fault-to-joint mapping is covered in [[heuristic--match-sprint-fault-to-rom-check-before-intervening]]. This entry is the *how*.
- **Thomas test (hip extension, passive).** Athlete on the table end, one knee to chest, other leg dropped. Read three things: *thigh height* (parallel, above or below the table), *thigh line* (in line with the body, drifting out, or rotated, which he reads as TFL, glute med or external rotators), *shin angle* (90°, obtuse or acute, where acute = "super tight quads"). "A lot of information in a short amount of time."
- **Hip flexion (passive, then active).** Move to end range and feel the end-feel. Watch the *other* hip: does it lift, does the knee bend? Ask where the athlete feels it; groin pinching is a flag. Active: how far can he bring the thigh up without cramping the hamstring, extending the knee, or rotating/cheating with the back? He bends the knee "to take the hamstrings out."
- **Hamstring, supine (passive, then active).** Something under the opposite knee to keep it in contact with the table. The athlete's hands under the lumbar spine so the low back cannot help. Hold ankle and knee, raise the leg. Judge range **and quality of tension**: it should build "like an escalator" (gradual), not "an elevator" (a sudden wall).
- **Hamstring at the knee, prone/standing (switching, long lever).** Shoulder–hip–knee in line. Passive: can he pull the heel to the butt? Active: using only the hamstrings, how high does the heel rise? Heel-to-butt gap wider than **pinky-to-thumb span** = work needed. Athletes often cramp. Some "could barely lift their foot off the ground." He says this test is missing from the hamstring literature.
- **Dorsiflexion (knee-to-wall).** Heel stays heavy. The knee tracks over the **third toe, not the big toe**, because "it's easy to cheat... when we go valgus." Adequate ≈ **4 inches** from the wall (his proxy for the "about 20° or more" figure he has seen, since he has no goniometer). Active: shin vertical, lift the forefoot. Measure foot-to-floor distance, not the shin–foot angle.
- **Straight-knee dorsiflexion / plantar flexion.** Knee held straight. "I believe the range of motion is supposed to be **30 to 35 degrees**" (it is unclear which motion he is quoting this for). Watch for inversion/eversion compensation. For plantar flexion: can he point straight? Pain in the Achilles region he calls a closed-angle joint issue.
- **Big toe.** Kneel, **hold the arch** to stop pronation or supination cheating, lift the toe passively, then actively. Watch for toe abduction and bunion drift.
- **Tibial rotation (toe-off fault, Live 3 ~55 min).** Supine: is the tibia in line with the femur, or turned out? Does it rotate out as the hip flexes? Active: can he internally and externally rotate the *tibia*, not the ankle?

**Why it works** — Each test isolates one joint while blocking the usual compensations: hands under the lumbar spine, the opposite knee pinned, the arch held, the knee over the third toe. The number you get then reflects that joint rather than the athlete's ability to cheat. Passive-then-active gives the gap that drives the treatment choice ([[heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint]]). The Thomas test and knee-to-wall are standard clinical tests. The thresholds and the escalator/elevator feel are Moyer's rules of thumb ("not very scientific, guys").

**When to apply** — Intake on any athlete whose sprint fault could have a range cause. It is quick enough to run in a small group inside a lift. In RTP, use the same procedures before and after a range block so re-tests match.

**When NOT to apply** — Where Baylor's Athletic Medicine staff already measure these with goniometry or validated knee-to-wall protocols, use their numbers rather than a hand-span. The thresholds are not validated, and end-feel judgement is subjective and differs between testers. Do not diagnose tibial torsion or other structural issues from these screens. That belongs to medical staff.

**Example** — Pre-camp for 12 DBs: Thomas test, prone active knee flexion and knee-to-wall, about 3 min per athlete. Three flag on active knee flexion (gap wider than a hand-span) and go to the hamstring PAILs/RAILs group. One reaches only 2 in on knee-to-wall and gets ankle range work before any projection drills.

# PAILs/RAILs to Close the Active–Passive Gap (Hamstring, Dorsiflexion)

**What it is** — Moyer's main tool for branch 2 of the range rule (passive range present, active range short). It is borrowed from FRC/FRS, which he names as his bias. His framing: range improves with **"time and/or tension."**
- **PAILs** (progressive angular isometric loading): at end range, the athlete contracts *into* the stretch. Hamstring version: lying with the leg raised, drive the foot down into a yoga block with the quads "like you're trying to break the block." Moyer's description of the muscles is garbled, but the intent is to push into the restriction.
- **RAILs** (regressive angular isometric loading): the athlete then uses the *opposite* muscles to pull further into range. Hamstring version: actively lift the foot with the hamstrings to close the gap. "This is where the cramps come." Athletes "cheat like a son of a bitch."
- **Dose:** PAILs holds of **20, 30, 40 or 60 s** depending on the athlete ("pretty gruesome for an isometric"). For teenagers he simplifies to **20 s PAILs / 10 s RAILs = one 30-s round**, set on kitchen timers, prescribing only the number of rounds.
- **Dorsiflexion version:** toes flexed up against a block, heel heavy, knee driven forward. PAILs = drive foot, ankle and toes down "like stepping on the gas". RAILs = lift the toes and foot while still pushing the knee forward.
- **Also used:** loaded stretches (single-leg standing and seated calf raises through full range; a seated cable-row "sit and reach" with heels driven in and feet actively dorsiflexed), a plantar-flexion stretch held for time, and PAILs/RAILs on it "if they're gluttons for punishment." Used for tibial rotation too, with hamstring and calf soft-tissue work, before he suspects posture.

**Why it works (as asserted)** — Isometric contraction at end range is said to build strength and tissue tolerance in the range the athlete cannot yet control, so active range catches up to passive. The RAILs phase trains the muscles that must hold the position in the sprint: the hamstrings folding the swing leg, the dorsiflexors at ground contact. That end-range isometrics can increase range is plausible and has some support in the stretching literature. The specific FRC protocol and Moyer's claim that he has "not seen any other system get better results" are unverified opinion.

**When to apply** — A football player with a long swing lever and a passive–active hamstring gap ([[case-study--nfl-running-back-long-lever-wearable-resistance-sprint]]); a projection or toe-off fault with restricted dorsiflexion that is not a bony block. It is simple to hand to a group: 20/10 × N rounds fits a warm-up or the end of a lift.

**When NOT to apply** — Early after a hamstring strain, maximal end-range isometrics into a healing tissue are a medical-staff decision, not an Athletic Performance default. Hard dorsiflexion loading is wrong when the limit is a bony or anterior impingement (his "closed-angle joint pain" flag). Cramping is expected, but cramping near a recent injury needs a clinician's call. There are no outcome data in the course. The only "result" is the long-lever case, which had several changes at once.

**Example** — Post-lift finisher for four DBs flagged on the prone active knee-flexion test: 4 rounds of 20 s PAILs / 10 s RAILs per leg on the hamstring, then 3 rounds on the dorsiflexion block. Re-test active knee flexion every two weeks with the same procedure ([[framework--sprint-rom-screen-thomas-hamstring-dorsiflexion]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint]] — this is the branch-2 tool.

# PAILs/RAILs to Close the Active–Passive Gap (Hamstring, Dorsiflexion)

**What it is** — Moyer's main tool for branch 2 of the range rule (passive range present, active range short). It is borrowed from FRC/FRS, which he names as his bias. His framing: range improves with **"time and/or tension."**
- **PAILs** (progressive angular isometric loading): at end range, the athlete contracts *into* the stretch. Hamstring version: lying with the leg raised, drive the foot down into a yoga block with the quads "like you're trying to break the block." Moyer's description of the muscles is garbled, but the intent is to push into the restriction.
- **RAILs** (regressive angular isometric loading): the athlete then uses the *opposite* muscles to pull further into range. Hamstring version: actively lift the foot with the hamstrings to close the gap. "This is where the cramps come." Athletes "cheat like a son of a bitch."
- **Dose:** PAILs holds of **20, 30, 40 or 60 s** depending on the athlete ("pretty gruesome for an isometric"). For teenagers he simplifies to **20 s PAILs / 10 s RAILs = one 30-s round**, set on kitchen timers, prescribing only the number of rounds.
- **Dorsiflexion version:** toes flexed up against a block, heel heavy, knee driven forward. PAILs = drive foot, ankle and toes down "like stepping on the gas". RAILs = lift the toes and foot while still pushing the knee forward.
- **Also used:** loaded stretches (single-leg standing and seated calf raises through full range; a seated cable-row "sit and reach" with heels driven in and feet actively dorsiflexed), a plantar-flexion stretch held for time, and PAILs/RAILs on it "if they're gluttons for punishment." Used for tibial rotation too, with hamstring and calf soft-tissue work, before he suspects posture.

**Why it works (as asserted)** — Isometric contraction at end range is said to build strength and tissue tolerance in the range the athlete cannot yet control, so active range catches up to passive. The RAILs phase trains the muscles that must hold the position in the sprint: the hamstrings folding the swing leg, the dorsiflexors at ground contact. That end-range isometrics can increase range is plausible and has some support in the stretching literature. The specific FRC protocol and Moyer's claim that he has "not seen any other system get better results" are unverified opinion.

**When to apply** — A football player with a long swing lever and a passive–active hamstring gap ([[case-study--nfl-running-back-long-lever-wearable-resistance-sprint]]); a projection or toe-off fault with restricted dorsiflexion that is not a bony block. It is simple to hand to a group: 20/10 × N rounds fits a warm-up or the end of a lift.

**When NOT to apply** — Early after a hamstring strain, maximal end-range isometrics into a healing tissue are a medical-staff decision, not an Athletic Performance default. Hard dorsiflexion loading is wrong when the limit is a bony or anterior impingement (his "closed-angle joint pain" flag). Cramping is expected, but cramping near a recent injury needs a clinician's call. There are no outcome data in the course. The only "result" is the long-lever case, which had several changes at once.

**Example** — Post-lift finisher for four DBs flagged on the prone active knee-flexion test: 4 rounds of 20 s PAILs / 10 s RAILs per leg on the hamstring, then 3 rounds on the dorsiflexion block. Re-test active knee flexion every two weeks with the same procedure ([[framework--sprint-rom-screen-thomas-hamstring-dorsiflexion]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint]] — this is the branch-2 tool.

# The Sprint Correctives Menu, Organised by Quality

**What it is** — Moyer's troubleshooting sheet (a PDF in the course, walked through in Lesson 9 and again in Live 3 ~1–60 min). For each global quality, the menu gives: the faults that flag it, what range to check first, then technical drills, cues, strength exercises and where to place wearable load. It is his menu, drawn from Yessis, Verkhoshansky, Natera and his own practice. He invites coaches to add their own.

| Quality | Faults that flag it | Check first | Technical drills | Cues | Strength | Wearable placement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Projection** | Short stride; little centre-of-mass travel | Hip extension (Thomas), hip flexion, dorsiflexion bent- and straight-knee, plantar flexion, big toe, all passive vs. active | Broad jumps (single/repeat); **heavy sled sprints** (load-velocity profiled), short accels; resisted bounding; wall acceleration drills → banded; heavy sled pushes (only if no room to sprint); leaps/bounds for distance | Push the ground away; push through the ground; stay on the ground as long as possible; explode; sprint up a hill; (Live 3) lead with your belt buckle, drive hips forward | Wall accels; hip extension (bridges); calf raises seated and standing, single and double leg (ankles are "more times than not" the limit); Yessis lunges (back leg straight, lead with hips), isometric holds if hip-extension range is short; banded front lunges (Active Cords); barbell front lunges; explosive front lunges | **Front of thigh + front of calf** |
| **Reactivity / stiffness** | Heel strike; poor trunk discipline (leaning, rounded); soft collapsing stance (ankle "mush"); knee locked at toe-off | Range "isn't usually going to be a problem"; this is a strength quality | Build-up sprints for frequency; overhead PVC/med-ball/arms-up sprints and wickets; single-leg jumps; extensive jumps; depth jumps (Verkhoshansky); pogos | Be quick off the ground; bounce; snap the ground like a whip | Yessis delay squats; K-Box (flywheel) squats; Natera ISO foot holds and mid-thigh pulls | **Vest (heavy, vertical load) + weights all around the ankle/calf** |
| **Switching: knee drive** | Low thigh height; long lever | Hip flexion; hamstring at the knee, passive vs. active | Dribbling drills; banded bounding; wicket runs (with wearable load); switch jumps (Live 3: band-resisted in a squat rack rather than over boxes) | Break the glass; throw a knee; sprint up a hill; drive the thigh hard | Yessis knee drives; Russian special strength; reverse crunches (lower abs, posterior tilt; build to 50 reps → ankle weights → band); explosive front lunge + knee drive; hamstring PAILs/RAILs for a long lever | **Front of thigh; posterior calf** (to force the fold) |
| **Switching: pawback** | Foot drops instead of attacking; lands far in front of hips; "straight down, not back and down" | Hip flexion; hamstrings | Scissor runs; banded bounding; banded marches; speed bounding; wicket runs; switch jumps | Snap the ground like a whip; hammer the nail; hit the ground hard | Yessis pawbacks; Natera ISO hamstrings; GHRs (setup: hamstring origin hanging *in front of* the pad for a double contraction); banded retractions (acceleration); bridges incl. single-leg; hip-flexion PAILs/RAILs | **Posterior shorts (hamstrings/glutes) + posterior calf** |
| **Toe-off (ankle extension)** | Knee extends at toe-off; foot turns out, pushing off the side of the foot | Dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, big toe; **tibial rotation** | "Bart walks" (banded low-lunge walks driving through the big toe; Chris Korfist's name for them is uncertain in the transcript); 45° banded walks/bounds | Push the ground away | Single-leg calf raises with the foot straight and pressure through the big toe; Natera foot isos (done "every day") | **Around the ankles**; for a turned-out foot, wrap calf loads **obliquely**, heavy end toward the medial malleolus |

Standing rules that go with the table: **sled sprints over sled pushes** when there is a choice (the only reason given for pushes is weather and space). **"Load the problem"** with wearable resistance. **If the foot turns out, check the tibia before any drills**, because "none of those technical drills... is going to work if the issue stems from the knee down."

**Why it works** — The menu puts one idea into operation. A global fault has several possible causes (range, strength, coordination, awareness), so it offers one or more options per cause and orders them range → drills/strength → cues/load. The pairing of each quality with its muscles and joint actions is taken from the course's biomechanics. That each exercise fixes its fault is Moyer's practice claim, supported by his before/after films, not by controlled comparison.

**When to apply** — Writing individual "first 10–15 minutes" add-ons inside a team lift. In Live 3 Moyer shows bucketing a 16-player group into four profile groups with 4–5 exercises each; see [[framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles]]. RTP late stages: pick the row that matches the athlete's pre-injury film fault. Staff education: it is a ready common language between Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a menu, not a diagnosis. Several rows share exercises (wickets, banded bounding, switch jumps), so a "fix" cannot confirm which cause was real. Several items rest on contested claims: the knee should stay bent at toe-off (disputed within the course); "posturology", i.e. an out-turned foot that PAILs/RAILs and soft-tissue work do not fix is "a postural issue" linked to "the feet and the eyes", which is his opinion with no evidence offered; and wearable placements are rules of thumb from a product he promotes. Heavy vest loading and depth jumps for stiffness need the landing and tissue tolerance a returning athlete may not yet have.

**Example** — A tight end lands with his foot far in front of his hips and drops it rather than attacking. Switching/pawback row: check hip-flexion and hamstring range (both fine). Then 2×/week banded pawbacks and GHRs, wicket runs with posterior-calf loading, and the cue "hammer the nail". Re-film in three weeks.

**Related** — [[heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint]] — decides whether the "check first" column or the drills columns apply; [[framework--isometric-set-positions-ankle-knee-hip]] — the Natera isometrics the menu links to.

# Choose Sprint Cues by Testing: Outcome First, Then Feel

**What it is** — Moyer's cueing rule: try several cues on the athlete and keep the one that (1) **produces the outcome** you want on film or the clock and (2) **makes the athlete feel** what you want. "Most of the time" he leans external ("pretend there's a pane of glass in front of you", "hammer the nail", "snap the ground like a whip", "sprint up a hill", "pretend the ground's on fire"). But he says "sometimes an internal focus works too. I'm not a big believer that it's all or nothing. The answer is usually in the middle." His preferred "cue" is often no words at all: **wickets**, which are an external constraint where "the fear of tripping... fear can be a great motivator" does the coaching. "All the cues in the world don't work as well as wickets" (Live 2). In Live 2 he pushes back on a track coach who cues the arms ("pull your arms through faster"). His objection is not that it is wrong ("I'm a resultist") but that it is an internal cue whose **long-term retention** is unknown, and that for football players he does not want them "thinking about their arms."

**Why it works** — Testing cues treats each athlete as an n-of-1: the words that change one athlete's action may do nothing for another, so outcome is the arbiter. The "feel" criterion comes from his motor-learning approach ([[heuristic--old-way-new-way-heel-strike-sprint]]). He wants a sensation the athlete can use to tell new from old. The rationale for wickets (a constraint that forces the action without attention to the body) fits the constraints-led account. The claim that internal cues sometimes work better is his experience, not tested in the course.

**When to apply** — Individual sprint work where one cue has not landed. Prefer external wording and physical constraints (wickets, a stick held overhead, a band) first. Keep internal cues as a fallback for athletes who ask for body-level detail. Always judge by the next rep's action, not by whether the athlete "got it."

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** The Myszka library entry reports a large literature (73 studies for performance, 40 for learning) favouring external focus, with durable retention. On that evidence, "the answer is in the middle" understates how one-sided the data are. Choosing the cue the athlete says *feels* best adds a second risk: felt improvement and actual change often differ, so outcome must stay the first test. Moyer's own "feel" emphasis leans internal. In the other direction, the external-focus literature is mostly lab and closed-skill tasks, and Moyer's point that some learners want body-level information is not refuted by it. Keep in-game cueing external and minimal. A football player mid-play should not be monitoring his shins.

**Example** — A receiver who sits in the ground at acceleration: "push the ground away" (no change), "sprint up a hill" (longer push, better film), "drive your knee" (athlete says it feels right, film unchanged). Keep "sprint up a hill". Add a wall-drill band for feel off the field.

**Related** — [[principle--external-focus-of-attention]] — tension: Myszka treats external focus as settled; Moyer is pluralist. Agreement on wickets and constraints as the best "cue"; see also [[principle--rate-limiters-and-fear]].
