# Choose Sprint Cues by Testing: Outcome First, Then Feel

**What it is** — Moyer's cueing rule: try several cues on the athlete and keep the one that (1) **produces the outcome** you want on film or the clock and (2) **makes the athlete feel** what you want. "Most of the time" he leans external ("pretend there's a pane of glass in front of you", "hammer the nail", "snap the ground like a whip", "sprint up a hill", "pretend the ground's on fire"). But he says "sometimes an internal focus works too. I'm not a big believer that it's all or nothing. The answer is usually in the middle." His preferred "cue" is often no words at all: **wickets**, which are an external constraint where "the fear of tripping... fear can be a great motivator" does the coaching. "All the cues in the world don't work as well as wickets" (Live 2). In Live 2 he pushes back on a track coach who cues the arms ("pull your arms through faster"). His objection is not that it is wrong ("I'm a resultist") but that it is an internal cue whose **long-term retention** is unknown, and that for football players he does not want them "thinking about their arms."

**Why it works** — Testing cues treats each athlete as an n-of-1: the words that change one athlete's action may do nothing for another, so outcome is the arbiter. The "feel" criterion comes from his motor-learning approach ([[heuristic--old-way-new-way-heel-strike-sprint]]). He wants a sensation the athlete can use to tell new from old. The rationale for wickets (a constraint that forces the action without attention to the body) fits the constraints-led account. The claim that internal cues sometimes work better is his experience, not tested in the course.

**When to apply** — Individual sprint work where one cue has not landed. Prefer external wording and physical constraints (wickets, a stick held overhead, a band) first. Keep internal cues as a fallback for athletes who ask for body-level detail. Always judge by the next rep's action, not by whether the athlete "got it."

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** The Myszka library entry reports a large literature (73 studies for performance, 40 for learning) favouring external focus, with durable retention. On that evidence, "the answer is in the middle" understates how one-sided the data are. Choosing the cue the athlete says *feels* best adds a second risk: felt improvement and actual change often differ, so outcome must stay the first test. Moyer's own "feel" emphasis leans internal. In the other direction, the external-focus literature is mostly lab and closed-skill tasks, and Moyer's point that some learners want body-level information is not refuted by it. Keep in-game cueing external and minimal. A football player mid-play should not be monitoring his shins.

**Example** — A receiver who sits in the ground at acceleration: "push the ground away" (no change), "sprint up a hill" (longer push, better film), "drive your knee" (athlete says it feels right, film unchanged). Keep "sprint up a hill". Add a wall-drill band for feel off the field.

**Related** — [[principle--external-focus-of-attention]] — tension: Myszka treats external focus as settled; Moyer is pluralist. Agreement on wickets and constraints as the best "cue"; see also [[principle--rate-limiters-and-fear]].

== principle--rate-limiters-and-fear
**What it is** — A **rate limiter** is an individual constraint that limits **the rate at which a performer acquires and develops a skill through exploration of the solution space** (Seifert et al., 2014; Moy et al., 2024). An individual constraint is any physical or psychological characteristic influencing the movement solutions available.

In football, the rate limiters the authors name for young players are **fear of being hit** and **fear of jamming one's fingers when catching.** Both **limit how far the player will explore.**
== principle--soft-assembly-and-learner-centred-coaching
**What it is** — The role change the whole framework demands. Coaches and specialists must **reconceptualise themselves as facilitators guiding a player's development, rather than as dictators constantly telling players how to think and act.**

**Learner-centred** means placing the athlete at the centre of the practice environment (Davids et al., 2008), which deepens their **knowledge of the performance landscape** — *in-game knowledge* (O'Sullivan et al., 2021) — and leads to greater adaptability.
== framework--ecological-dynamics-athlete-environment
**What it is** — A theoretical framework, assembled around 2006 by Keith Davids and Duarte Araújo from ecology, psychology, human movement science, nonlinear dynamics and mathematics. Its defining commitment: **the person and the environment are equally important, and neither can be understood without the other.** The unit of analysis is the relationship, not the athlete.

This section of the book is written by Davids and Araújo themselves, and they place it against two predecessors:
== principle--knowledge-of-vs-knowledge-about
**What it is** — Gibson's (1966) distinction, and one of the sharpest diagnostic tools in the book.

**Knowledge *about*** is conceptual and indirect. It is demonstrated verbally or through symbols and pictures — a play drawn on a whiteboard, a coverage explained, a film clip discussed. It is **scaled in units of physics** ("when you are 10 yards from the receiver") rather than to the player's own body, because it refers to the typical and the ideal. In terms of action it can only describe *what to perceive* and *what to do*.
== principle--movement-ownership-speed
**What it is** — Deliberately operating at a **maximum controllable speed** rather than a maximum speed. The glossary definition: intentionally operating at a velocity deemed maximally controllable, instead of always practising or playing at the highest speeds attainable, so the player can better coordinate and control the most functional solution to a peculiar problem.

The authors know it sounds wrong for football, and argue it anyway. Of course there are moments demanding maximal burst, deceleration or change of direction. But **a player always running around like their hair is on fire — a way of being that football coaches celebrate and reward — can miss perceptual connection to the very information specifying the affordances for the biggest plays.**

# Motor Control Theories Are Tools: Pick by Athlete and Task

**What it is** — Moyer's stance on the motor-control theory wars. Theories (reflex, hierarchical, motor program, dynamic/complex systems, ecological) are **tools, not creeds**, and the one to use depends on **context**: who the athlete is, what their current skill and body awareness are, what feedback they prefer (verbal, visual, sensory), whether they want guidance or discovery, and whether the goal is **adaptability** or **fixing one specific element of technique**. His authority is Mark Latash (Penn State; translator and editor of Bernstein's work, 2007 Bernstein Prize, founding editor of *Motor Control*), whom he quotes from personal emails: "dynamical systems theory, hierarchy, ecological approach — these words emphasize certain aspects of the actual system, which combines them all... the control scheme is of course hierarchical and it deals with a dynamic system... most actions are ecologically sensible." Moyer reads "most" as "not all." His critique of the constraints-led camp: they cite Bernstein's blacksmiths to argue for variability, "but not a lot of us are working with blacksmiths". Novices "don't know their ass from their elbow" and cannot be expected to self-organise a solution. His analogy: you would not hand a kid every tool and say "build me a bench" without first teaching what each tool does. "Only Sith Lords work in absolutes."

**Why it works** — Different theories describe different levels of the same system (Latash's point). So a practitioner can borrow the hierarchical/instructional view when an athlete lacks basic awareness of a pattern, and the ecological view when the goal is adapting skill to the game. Moyer puts this into practice as a *sequence*: explicit, isolated learning first, then constraints-led and differential learning once the pattern is stable ([[framework--isolate-integrate-improvise-sprint-technique]]). The reasoning is his. Latash's quote supports theoretical pluralism about *description*, not Moyer's specific coaching sequence.

**When to apply** — Deciding how to coach a *specific technical fault* (heel strike, long lever) in an athlete who has done it for years. There, explicit awareness work plus special exercises is Moyer's default. Also useful for mediating staff arguments ("CLA vs. drills"): ask what the athlete and the goal are before arguing method.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested, in both directions.** From the ecological side (Myszka, Davids & Araújo), theories are not interchangeable toolkits. They make incompatible claims about what learning *is* (stored programs vs. attunement to information), and "pick by context" can become a licence to keep decontextualised drilling. The CLA authors also do not claim novices should be left to "chaos". Task simplification is their answer for novices. Moyer caricatures that position. From Moyer's side, the ecological authors' own evidence mostly concerns *game skills with opponents*, not closed-cycle sprint mechanics in an athlete with an entrenched pattern. That is where his case for explicit correction is strongest. Also note: "context matters" is compatible with almost any practice, so it cannot by itself justify one.

**Example** — A true-freshman DB with a lifelong heel strike gets explicit old-way/new-way work and special exercises for three weeks. A veteran receiver whose mechanics are fine but who loses speed at the catch point gets chase and ball-in-flight games instead. Two athletes, two tools, one staff.

**Related** — [[framework--ecological-dynamics-athlete-environment]] and [[principle--soft-assembly-and-learner-centred-coaching]] — tension: Myszka commits to one theory; Moyer is pluralist. [[claim--there-is-no-muscle-memory]] — tension with Moyer's "ingrained program" language.

# "Old Way / New Way": Changing an Ingrained Sprint Pattern With the Athlete's Own Words

**What it is** — Moyer's method for changing a long-standing fault. His worked case is heel striking, which he calls the most common fault in his facility. It is a contrast method from Australia (he cites three papers without naming authors in the transcript). The obstacle it targets is **proactive interference**: the old, long-practised pattern interferes with learning a similar new one. Moyer calls it "proactive inhibition", then describes interference. It does not stop learning. It makes the old solution come back, so "you can give an athlete a cue... and in that drill they can demonstrate it, but as soon as you give them that same drill or a cognitive task they go right back." The procedure:
1. **Explain why** the change matters (his framing: mediated learning and constructivism).
2. Athlete runs the **new way** (e.g., midfoot/forefoot landing, jog down and back) and describes **in their own adjectives** what it felt like: usually "weird", "bouncy", "on my toes", "leaning forward".
3. Athlete runs the **old way** and describes that. Then new again, old again.
4. The athlete's own words become the coaching vocabulary: "If it doesn't feel weird or bouncy, you're probably doing it the old way." Labels are **old/new, never right/wrong**.
5. **Special-strength "sandwich":** run old/new outside → come in for special strength exercises (Yessis Active Cords, knee drives, pawbacks, wearable load) targeting the action → go back out and run old/new. Athletes commonly report it "feels so much easier." Moyer calls that response "gold."

**Why it works (as asserted)** — The theory he offers, with rough neuroscience ("sensory cortex drives motor cortex drives prefrontal cortex"): metacognition and **discriminative learning** make the difference between the two patterns something the athlete can perceive and name, so they can catch the old pattern themselves. The special exercises strengthen the key action and add sensory input, which he says makes the new pattern easier to feel. The contrast/discrimination idea has real support in the motor-learning literature. The brain-region explanation and his "right-brain/left-brain" learner typing (via a Human Information Processing survey he no longer can buy) are not well supported and should not be cited.

**When to apply** — An athlete with a years-old, specific fault that is still there after drills and cues, such as a heel-striking freshman or a receiver who drops his foot. It suits RTP too: an athlete returning after a lower-limb injury who has adopted a guarded pattern can use old/new contrast to find and drop the compensation.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** The method directs attention *internally*, to how the body feels, and adds conscious control early. The external-focus literature in the Myszka entries predicts that this will hurt performance and may slow automatisation. In the other direction, Moyer's use is diagnostic and temporary (contrast to discover, then move to integration and games), and the external-focus studies rarely test unlearning an entrenched pattern. That is the specific problem proactive interference poses. Separately, the premise that **heel striking is bad and midfoot is "more efficient"** is itself an untested causal claim in the course, and so is his injury link (see [[claim--heel-striking-flags-non-contact-running-injury]]). Confirm on film that the athlete actually lands with heel-first loading at sprint speed before "fixing" it. Finally, "it feels better" is the athlete's report, not evidence the action changed. Re-film.

**Example** — A freshman corner heel-strikes on build-ups. He runs two old/new pairs and names the new way "bouncy and tall". Then 3×8 banded pawbacks and knee drives, then two more pairs. Film shows forefoot contact on the new-way runs, and the cue for the rest of the block is "bouncy and tall." Contrast runs continue at the start of the next sessions to check the new pattern has held ([[heuristic--check-retention-not-cue-delivery-sprint]]).

**Related** — [[principle--external-focus-of-attention]] — tension (internal feel vs external focus); [[claim--there-is-no-muscle-memory]] — tension with the "deeply ingrained program" framing; [[heuristic--semi-structured-player-interviews]] — agreement: both draw on the athlete's own account.

**What it is** — Moyer's three-stage progression for a changed technique (from Ido Portal's "3 I" framing; Moyer calls it "breaking bad"). Worked example: heel strike → midfoot/forefoot.

Move up only if the new pattern holds with "technical proficiency." Slow to fast, short to long. "Learning isn't done at 100% speed", because "you lose sensory information" at max speed, and mechanics change with velocity.
2. **Integrate.** Only after **repeated 100% sprints across multiple sessions** hold the pattern, add complexity **slowly**, one stimulus at a time: arms overhead → shoulders and head turned while the legs run straight → arms across chest → holding a stick or ball → being chased in a straight line → chasing someone in a straight line.
3. **Improvise.** Zig-zag chases, changing directions while chasing or being chased, catching or kicking a ball. Then small-sided → medium → large-sided games that "resemble a practice." Here he switches to a "nonlinear... differential learning, constraints-led, ecological approach" and perception–action coupling.
**The regression rule:** if a new stimulus brings back the old pattern (e.g., chasing a teammate, "now they're not thinking about heel striking"), **scale back complexity**. The pattern has not yet moved from conscious competence to unconscious competence.

**Why it works (as asserted)** — Early on, the new pattern needs attention. Any competing demand (speed, a ball, an opponent) takes attention away, and the old pattern, which is stronger, wins (proactive interference). Adding demands one at a time lets the new pattern become robust to each before the next. The staging and the "conscious → unconscious competence" idea are practitioner models. Moyer shows before/after film but no controlled comparison.

**When to apply** — Sprint-technique changes in any football player. It maps cleanly onto late-stage RTP: straight-line %-effort ramps (already standard in return-to-run) → sport-specific constraints (ball, turned head, pursuit angles) → reactive, opposed drills → team periods. The regression rule gives a clear decision point: if the old pattern returns in a reactive drill, go back a step rather than pushing through.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** The Myszka authors argue that isolating a skill from its information (the straight-line, unopposed isolate stage) teaches attunement to the wrong information, and that task *simplification* (keep a chaser, change the distance) beats *decomposition*. On their evidence, the isolate stage should be brief or should keep a chaser from the start. Moyer's counter is that his isolate stage targets a *mechanical* fault in a closed, cyclic action, where "the information" is largely internal. And the CLA studies test game skills, not unlearning an entrenched pattern. Neither side has direct evidence for sprint-pattern change. And his integrate list is arbitrary in order. Choose stimuli that match the athlete's position.

**Example** — A DB fixing a heel strike. Weeks 1–2: 50/75/90/100% build-ups with old/new contrast. Week 3: backpedal-turn-and-run with head over the shoulder, then pursuit of a ball-carrier on a fixed angle. Week 4: 1v1 open-field tag in a 10×10 yd box. # Judge a Sprint Intervention by Whether the Action Changed and Stayed Changed

**What it is** — A thread across Lesson 10 and the live sessions. Three checks follow from it:
1. **The action changed, not the cue delivered.** Giving a cue is not coaching. The test is whether the next rep *looks* different on film. Moyer's standard for any coach: "show me the before, tell me what the intervention was, and let's see what we got."
2. **Immediate change ≠ learning.** On an arm-action cue in Live 2: "What is the long-term retention of that learning from that one cue?... Learning's done through retention. If they can replicate it in the next run, awesome. But what about next week?" In Live 3, he adds that an athlete can show a cued change in the drill, then revert "as soon as you give them that same drill or a cognitive task."
3. **Fade the support and see if the action holds.** His wicket fade: after a run of **10–15 wickets**, remove the **last five** and tell the athlete to keep running "as if they were still there". Then remove the next five. Hurdles have to go eventually, "they're not sprinting a hurdle."

**Why it works** — Performance during practice reflects temporary support: the cue in working memory, the wicket forcing the fold. Learning is what remains when the support is gone and time has passed. This performance/learning distinction is well established in motor-learning research. Moyer's fade gives a within-session transfer test: the wicket-free section shows whether the athlete can produce the action from the feel alone.

**When to apply** — Evaluating any technical intervention, including your own: re-film the *next session*, not just the next rep. In RTP, a mechanic that appears only straight after a cue should not count as restored. Wicket and band progressions should always have a planned fade.

**When NOT to apply** — Moyer undercuts this himself by treating "that feels better" as "gold". An athlete's report is an *immediate* signal and often does not match the film. Use it to pick the next rep, not to judge learning. A retention check a week later is also confounded by fatigue and by whatever else changed that week. Compare like with like (same distance, timing, fatigue state). Finally, this is not an argument against cues: a cue that only works acutely can still be useful as a pre-rep reminder.

**Example** — Tuesday: a receiver runs 12 wickets with good fold, then 3 reps with the last 4 removed. Film shows the fold holds for two steps past the last wicket. Thursday: fly-20 with no wickets, filmed from the side. The fold is there on two of three reps, so the change is partly retained. Keep the wicket block for another week before fading further.

**Related** — [[principle--repetition-without-repetition]] — agreement that practising one fixed movement is not the target; [[framework--three-training-effects]] — the immediate/delayed/cumulative split, applied here to skill rather than fitness.

# Motor Control Theories Are Tools: Pick by Athlete and Task

**What it is** — Moyer's stance on the motor-control theory wars. Theories (reflex, hierarchical, motor program, dynamic/complex systems, ecological) are **tools, not creeds**, and the one to use depends on **context**: who the athlete is, what their current skill and body awareness are, what feedback they prefer (verbal, visual, sensory), whether they want guidance or discovery, and whether the goal is **adaptability** or **fixing one specific element of technique**. His authority is Mark Latash (Penn State; translator and editor of Bernstein's work, 2007 Bernstein Prize, founding editor of *Motor Control*), whom he quotes from personal emails: "dynamical systems theory, hierarchy, ecological approach — these words emphasize certain aspects of the actual system, which combines them all... the control scheme is of course hierarchical and it deals with a dynamic system... most actions are ecologically sensible." Moyer reads "most" as "not all." His critique of the constraints-led camp: they cite Bernstein's blacksmiths to argue for variability, "but not a lot of us are working with blacksmiths". Novices "don't know their ass from their elbow" and cannot be expected to self-organise a solution. His analogy: you would not hand a kid every tool and say "build me a bench" without first teaching what each tool does. "Only Sith Lords work in absolutes."

**Why it works** — Different theories describe different levels of the same system (Latash's point). So a practitioner can borrow the hierarchical/instructional view when an athlete lacks basic awareness of a pattern, and the ecological view when the goal is adapting skill to the game. Moyer puts this into practice as a *sequence*: explicit, isolated learning first, then constraints-led and differential learning once the pattern is stable ([[framework--isolate-integrate-improvise-sprint-technique]]). The reasoning is his. Latash's quote supports theoretical pluralism about *description*, not Moyer's specific coaching sequence.

**When to apply** — Deciding how to coach a *specific technical fault* (heel strike, long lever) in an athlete who has done it for years. There, explicit awareness work plus special exercises is Moyer's default. Also useful for mediating staff arguments ("CLA vs. drills"): ask what the athlete and the goal are before arguing method.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested, in both directions.** From the ecological side (Myszka, Davids & Araújo), theories are not interchangeable toolkits. They make incompatible claims about what learning *is* (stored programs vs. attunement to information), and "pick by context" can become a licence to keep decontextualised drilling. The CLA authors also do not claim novices should be left to "chaos". Task simplification is their answer for novices. Moyer caricatures that position. From Moyer's side, the ecological authors' own evidence mostly concerns *game skills with opponents*, not closed-cycle sprint mechanics in an athlete with an entrenched pattern. That is where his case for explicit correction is strongest. Also note: "context matters" is compatible with almost any practice, so it cannot by itself justify one.

**Example** — A true-freshman DB with a lifelong heel strike gets explicit old-way/new-way work and special exercises for three weeks. A veteran receiver whose mechanics are fine but who loses speed at the catch point gets chase and ball-in-flight games instead. Two athletes, two tools, one staff.

**Related** — [[framework--ecological-dynamics-athlete-environment]] and [[principle--soft-assembly-and-learner-centred-coaching]] — tension: Myszka commits to one theory; Moyer is pluralist. [[claim--there-is-no-muscle-memory]] — tension with Moyer's "ingrained program" language.

# "Old Way / New Way": Changing an Ingrained Sprint Pattern With the Athlete's Own Words

2. Athlete runs the **new way** (e.g., midfoot/forefoot landing, jog down and back) and describes **in their own adjectives** what it felt like: usually "weird", "bouncy", "on my toes", "leaning forward".
3. Athlete runs the **old way** and describes that. Then new again, old again.
4. The athlete's own words become the coaching vocabulary: "If it doesn't feel weird or bouncy, you're probably doing it the old way." Labels are **old/new, never right/wrong**.

# Judge a Sprint Intervention by Whether the Action Changed and Stayed Changed

**What it is** — A thread across Lesson 10 and the live sessions. Three checks follow from it:
1. **The action changed, not the cue delivered.** Giving a cue is not coaching. The test is whether the next rep *looks* different on film. Moyer's standard for any coach: "show me the before, tell me what the intervention was, and let's see what we got."
2. **Immediate change ≠ learning.** On an arm-action cue in Live 2: "What is the long-term retention of that learning from that one cue?... Learning's done through retention. If they can replicate it in the next run, awesome. But what about next week?" In Live 3, he adds that an athlete can show a cued change in the drill, then revert "as soon as you give them that same drill or a cognitive task."
3. **Fade the support and see if the action holds.** His wicket fade: after a run of **10–15 wickets**, remove the **last five** and tell the athlete to keep running "as if they were still there". Then remove the next five. Hurdles have to go eventually, "they're not sprinting a hurdle."

**Why it works** — Performance during practice reflects temporary support: the cue in working memory, the wicket forcing the fold. Learning is what remains when the support is gone and time has passed. This performance/learning distinction is well established in motor-learning research. Moyer's fade gives a within-session transfer test: the wicket-free section shows whether the athlete can produce the action from the feel alone.

**When to apply** — Evaluating any technical intervention, including your own: re-film the *next session*, not just the next rep. In RTP, a mechanic that appears only straight after a cue should not count as restored. Wicket and band progressions should always have a planned fade.

**When NOT to apply** — Moyer undercuts this himself by treating "that feels better" as "gold". An athlete's report is an *immediate* signal and often does not match the film. Use it to pick the next rep, not to judge learning. A retention check a week later is also confounded by fatigue and by whatever else changed that week. Compare like with like (same distance, timing, fatigue state). Finally, this is not an argument against cues: a cue that only works acutely can still be useful as a pre-rep reminder.

**Example** — Tuesday: a receiver runs 12 wickets with good fold, then 3 reps with the last 4 removed. Film shows the fold holds for two steps past the last wicket. Thursday: fly-20 with no wickets, filmed from the side. The fold is there on two of three reps, so the change is partly retained. Keep the wicket block for another week before fading further.

**Related** — [[principle--repetition-without-repetition]] — agreement that practising one fixed movement is not the target; [[framework--three-training-effects]] — the immediate/delayed/cumulative split, applied here to skill rather than fitness.

14	# NFL Running Back With a Long Swing Lever: ROM Work, Posterior-Calf Loading, Wickets
15	
16	**What it is** — Moyer's flagship single-athlete case, told in Lesson 8 and filled in during Live 3, where the athlete is named as Najee Harris ("Naji" in the transcript). The athlete was an NFL running back, **245 lb** (the transcript also says "fixed two", probably a height such as 6'2"; unclear). **Problem:** he swung a long lever with one leg (Live 3 says the left). He struggled to fold the leg and struggled with knee-drive exercises. **Assessment (Live 3):** his active hamstring range was very poor: he could not lift his heel toward his butt with the hamstrings in prone, and the gap was well beyond Moyer's pinky-to-thumb threshold ([[framework--sprint-rom-screen-thomas-hamstring-dorsiflexion]]). **Interventions** reported across the two lessons: hamstring PAILs/RAILs to close the active–passive gap; LILA calf sleeves loaded on the **posterior calf** ("load the problem"; his thighs were too big for the shorts); knee-drive special strength; and wicket runs, which the athlete asked for as a former high-school track athlete, later faded by removing hurdles and combined with wearable load. **Reported outcome (Lesson 8):** in **one month**, his **flying-10** time improved by what the transcript renders as "500th" (most likely five hundredths of a second; unconfirmed), "doing nothing but sprinting and using Lila's." On film the lever shortened. He liked the sleeves enough to wear them in NFL practices.
17	
18	**Why it works** — As claimed: Moyer's account: the posterior-calf load increases the demand on the hamstrings to fold the leg and on the ankle, and the extra sensory input makes the fold something the athlete can feel. PAILs/RAILs gave him the active range to fold at all. Wickets use the fear of clipping a hurdle to force front-side mechanics without a cue.
19	
20	**When to apply** — As a template of *reasoning* for a football player with a long lever: film → check active vs. passive hamstring and hip-flexion range → close the range gap → strength in range → a constraint that forces the fold → fade the constraint → re-time. The order transfers well to RTP after a hamstring strain, where a long lever is also one of Moyer's hamstring-risk hypotheses.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Not evidence that wearable resistance works. It is one athlete. The Lesson 8 phrase "doing nothing but sprinting and using Lila's" conflicts with the Live 3 account of PAILs/RAILs, knee drives and wickets. There was no control, no stated timing method, and a flying-10 change of ~0.05 s is within the day-to-day variation of many timing setups. A month of focused sprinting alone would be expected to help an NFL back coming off a season. The equipment is Moyer's own, and he promotes the product. The athlete is identifiable. Cite the reasoning, not the result.
23	
24	**Example** — Baylor application: a transfer RB with a visible long lever on the left and a hamstring history gets the same sequence. He gets prone active knee-flexion testing, a PAILs/RAILs block, posterior-calf loading on selected sprints, and wickets with a planned fade. Fly-10 is timed on the same system before and after, with the other changes logged so the result is interpretable.
25	
26	**Related** — [[claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]]; [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]] — the risk hypothesis this case is used to illustrate.

14	# Light Wearable Resistance "Out-Energises" a Heavy Squat — Claim, and Why the Numbers Fail
15	
16	**What it is** — Moyer argues that very light, limb-mounted wearable resistance (LILA Exogen, loads "only in grams") is unusually powerful for sprint technique and speed. His mechanism is kinetic energy. As spoken in Lesson 8: a **100 kg back squat** gives kinetic energy of **"17.4 kg meters per second"**, while **one gram of LILA on the calves** gives **"18.6 kg per meter per second."** A barbell moves at about 1 m/s even in "speed squats", whereas the load on a sprinting limb moves at sprint speed ("eight, nine, ten meters per second"). So wearable load "keeps acceleration high" and "flips the force equation on its head." He cites John Cronin's work on upper- and lower-body wearable loading and acceleration kinematics as support. In Live 3 [00:00:01] he **retracts the arithmetic**: "Sorry, I fucked up the physics equation for the Lila's... that was Dr. John Cronin that did that so you can ask him." He keeps the conclusion.
17	
18	**Why it works** — As asserted: Kinetic energy is ½mv². Velocity is squared, so a small mass moving fast can carry energy comparable to a large mass moving slowly. Loading the distal limb also raises the limb's moment of inertia about the hip, which increases the demand on the hip flexors, the hamstrings and the knee drive and pawback ("load the problem"). That second mechanism is plausible and matches the placement rules in [[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]]. It is not the energy argument, though.
19	
20	**When to apply** — As a hypothesis to test, with realistic loads: a small, placement-specific overload of the swing limb at sprint speed. Useful as a CE-class tool ([[framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories]]) when you want sprint-speed overload without a sled changing posture.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Do not repeat the squat-vs-wearable comparison. It is wrong in three separate ways. (1) **Units:** "kg·m/s" is momentum, not energy (energy is joules, kg·m²/s²). (2) **Magnitude:** 17.4 J for 100 kg implies a bar speed of ~0.59 m/s, which is plausible. But 18.6 J from **1 g** needs a limb speed of about **190 m/s**. Even at a realistic peak foot speed (~20 m/s), 1 g carries ~0.2 J, and a heavier real load (~200 g) carries tens of joules. The comparison is dimensionally and numerically inconsistent as spoken. (3) **Concept:** "acceleration of 8–9 m/s" confuses velocity with acceleration. Beyond the physics, "faster sprinting from wearable resistance" is a transfer claim: Cronin's studies (not checked here) describe acute kinematic and kinetic changes, and acute change is not proof of chronic speed gains. **Conflict of interest:** Moyer uses and promotes LILA heavily ("yes, those are my Lila's"), and the course's `_book.md` notes that he sells wearable-resistance coaching. Supporting cases are single athletes with other interventions running at the same time ([[case-study--nfl-running-back-long-lever-wearable-resistance-sprint]]).
23	
24	**Example** — A staff member proposes buying wearable-resistance kits for the WR room because "a few grams beats a 100 kg squat." The correct response: the physics claim is broken. The limb-inertia mechanism is plausible. The purchase should hinge on a within-athlete trial with a measured outcome (fly-10, contact position on film), not the energy slide.

15	
16	**What it is** — Moyer's main tool for branch 2 of the range rule (passive range present, active range short). It is borrowed from FRC/FRS, which he names as his bias. His framing: range improves with **"time and/or tension."**
17	- **PAILs** (progressive angular isometric loading): at end range, the athlete contracts *into* the stretch. Hamstring version: lying with the leg raised, drive the foot down into a yoga block with the quads "like you're trying to break the block." Moyer's description of the muscles is garbled, but the intent is to push into the restriction.
18	- **RAILs** (regressive angular isometric loading): the athlete then uses the *opposite* muscles to pull further into range. Hamstring version: actively lift the foot with the hamstrings to close the gap. "This is where the cramps come." Athletes "cheat like a son of a bitch."
19	- **Dose:** PAILs holds of **20, 30, 40 or 60 s** depending on the athlete ("pretty gruesome for an isometric"). For teenagers he simplifies to **20 s PAILs / 10 s RAILs = one 30-s round**, set on kitchen timers, prescribing only the number of rounds.
20	- **Dorsiflexion version:** toes flexed up against a block, heel heavy, knee driven forward. PAILs = drive foot, ankle and toes down "like stepping on the gas". RAILs = lift the toes and foot while still pushing the knee forward.
21	- **Also used:** loaded stretches (single-leg standing and seated calf raises through full range; a seated cable-row "sit and reach" with heels driven in and feet actively dorsiflexed), a plantar-flexion stretch held for time, and PAILs/RAILs on it "if they're gluttons for punishment." Used for tibial rotation too, with hamstring and calf soft-tissue work, before he suspects posture.
22	
23	**Why it works** — As asserted: Isometric contraction at end range is said to build strength and tissue tolerance in the range the athlete cannot yet control, so active range catches up to passive. The RAILs phase trains the muscles that must hold the position in the sprint: the hamstrings folding the swing leg, the dorsiflexors at ground contact. That end-range isometrics can increase range is plausible and has some support in the stretching literature. The specific FRC protocol and Moyer's claim that he has "not seen any other system get better results" are unverified opinion.
24	
25	**When to apply** — A football player with a long swing lever and a passive–active hamstring gap ([[case-study--nfl-running-back-long-lever-wearable-resistance-sprint]]); a projection or toe-off fault with restricted dorsiflexion that is not a bony block. It is simple to hand to a group: 20/10 × N rounds fits a warm-up or the end of a lift.
26	
27	**When NOT to apply** — Early after a hamstring strain, maximal end-range isometrics into a healing tissue are a medical-staff decision, not an Athletic Performance default. Hard dorsiflexion loading is wrong when the limit is a bony or anterior impingement (his "closed-angle joint pain" flag). Cramping is expected, but cramping near a recent injury needs a clinician's call. There are no outcome data in the course. The only "result" is the long-lever case, which had several changes at once.
28	
29	**Example** — Post-lift finisher for four DBs flagged on the prone active knee-flexion test: 4 rounds of 20 s PAILs / 10 s RAILs per leg on the hamstring, then 3 rounds on the dorsiflexion block. Re-test active knee flexion every two weeks with the same procedure ([[framework--sprint-rom-screen-thomas-hamstring-dorsiflexion]]).
30	
31	**Related** — [[heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint]] — this is the branch-2 tool.
